title: You Must Become Smaller
author: We Made People
summary: The author, a first-generation church planter, argues that succession — deliberately shrinking one's own centrality so an organization can outlast its founder — is the true test of whether a leader's legacy is actually about the mission or about their own ego. Using the founding of East River Church as a case study, he describes how his original vision immediately broadened the moment his co-laborer David Pryor and wife Becky joined, and how the church's culture became something no single person's product. He contrasts this with 'high-profile failures' in his theological circles where a leader entangled a ministry so completely with himself that it could not survive his fall, arguing that legacy tied to a single person cannot outgrow that person and therefore cannot truly last. The piece closes with an extended metaphor: to see the work increase, the leader must embrace decreasing, framing succession planning as a discipline of sacrificing hubris and ego rather than a late-career administrative task.
points: The core argument — that a leader's legacy only truly lasts to the extent the leader becomes a smaller part of it — inverts the common assumption that legacy is built by maximizing personal visibility and centrality within an organization.

The East River Church case (the founder's original vision immediately broadening the moment co-founders joined) demonstrates succession as something that begins at founding, not as a late-stage handoff planned only near retirement or departure.

The 'high-profile failures' example, where ministries collapsed because leaders entangled their legacy with themselves so tightly that 'it could never grow past them,' identifies personal entanglement as the specific mechanism by which legacies fail to survive their founder.

Framing succession as requiring the leader to 'sacrifice hubris and ego so that something else can grow' reframes succession planning as a character discipline rather than a purely administrative or organizational-design exercise.
quotes: I would say succession is something that uniquely preoccupies my mind. I am the first, or the first in a long time, to do a lot of things on both sides of my family. And I am definitely a first-generation Christian.

But there is an odd paradox at play that I've discovered. If a man's legacy is to grow the right way, he will become a smaller part of it. Maybe an integral part, but still, what once was pages about him will, Lord willing, become a sentence or maybe two.

Immediately, the vision I had for East River broadened to include David and Becky's personalities and gifts. He and I are both particular in our own ways, and one of the reasons East River has a very different vibe is because it's not the product of a single individual.

Succession requires that you sacrifice your hubris and ego so that something else can grow and involve other people. It is one of the great tests of whether something is about you or about others and the Lord.
I am willing to go out on a limb and say they wanted a great legacy, yet they entangled it with themselves, and therefore it could never grow past them. They became their own limitation.
To see the work increase, you must embrace decreasing. And there's a lot of freedom in that.
